data.title: Ashland edges higher on report bids due this month
data.description:
Ashland ticked higher by almost 1% amid a report that the chemical maker is collecting takeover bids this month.

Apollo Global and Carlyle Group are among the financial sponsors interested in Ashland , according to traders, who cited a DealReporter article that was circulating on Tuesday.

The update comes after Bloomberg reported last month that the chemical maker was evaluating a possible sale after getting takeover interest. Advent, Apollo, and Carlyle Group () are among those that have had contact with the company.

Standard Industries Inc., which, through its investment platform Standard Investments LLC is among Ashland’s biggest shareholders, is also interested, according to the Bloomberg report.

A potential deal comes as activist investors have been pushing for months for Ashland to explore a sale. Last month, Ashland confirmed an agreement with activist investor Ancora Holdings to expand the chemical maker's board.

Ashland is set to hold its innovation day on Thursday.

data.title: PSP Investments CEO Orida Signals Interest in Canada Airports
data.description:
By Paul Vieira

OTTAWA--The chief executive of one of Canada's biggest pension funds with experience in transport logistics abroad said she is interested in striking a deal with Ottawa to invest in the country's biggest airports.

"We're well suited for the opportunity," Deborah Orida, president and CEO of the Public Service Pension Investment Board, said in an interview Tuesday on the sidelines at an investment summit hosted by Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney. Earlier in the day, Carney said Canada is ready to open the doors for private-sector investment in the country's four biggest airports, with cash raised to be deployed in crucial infrastructure that Canada needs.

The pension fund, also known as PSP Investments, owns seven airports, mostly in Europe, through its AviAlliance subsidiary. "We are not only an airport investor but also an airport operator," Orida said. "That makes us, I think, well positioned to participate."

PSP Investments has 320 billion Canadian dollars (US$230.2 billion) under management, and in 2025 delivered a one-year net return of 6.5% and a 10-year net annualized return of 8.8%. It is tasked with delivering returns for federal-government employees, members of the Canadian military and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

As envisaged by Carney, the airport deals would be set up as long-term concessions, which are agreements under which the private-sector investor handles the operation and maintenance of the airport for a set period. Current Canadian laws dissuade private-sector investments in airports, which are run by not-for-profit, non-share capital authorities that fund operations through fees charged to passengers and airlines.

Orida said PSP's AviAlliance has a track record that shows it can modernize airport terminals and expand route networks through its contact with airlines. The airports in the PSP portfolio include those in Athens, Glasgow and San Juan, Puerto Rico.

"We have the opportunity with our operating expertise to generate value that is not coming at the expense of the customers," Orida said. She added that the airports are a key holding in their infrastructure class, which over a five-year period has recorded average annual returns of about 15%.

According to Statistics Canada, the country's airports served 158.9 million passengers last year, with Toronto's Pearson International by far the largest, accounting for nearly 30% of passenger traffic.

The prior Liberal government administration, under former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, had an interest in encouraging more domestic investment by pension funds--drawing criticism from some pension-fund executives about any formal effort to compel asset managers to reallocate money from higher-returning opportunities.

Orida said Carney's airport announcement signals the government is looking to make good-investment opportunities more readily available for large investors like PSP. Prior to the summit, PSP unveiled plans to increase its domestic holdings by up to 40%, and cross the C$100 billion threshold in the next few years.

That pledge was driven by private-investing opportunities, "and the attractiveness of the Canadian public equities for our portfolio, rather than a government edict," she said.

Canada's largest pension fund, the CPP Investment Board, said Tuesday it would join forces with Brookfield Asset Management on a C$50 billion fund seeking opportunities in infrastructure. Prior to the summit, the five biggest Canadian banks pledged a collective C$320 billion in capital for the domestic economy.

Write to Paul Vieira at paul.vieira@wsj.com

data.title: Goldman Drops as $11.7 Billion Fundraise Tests Its Private-Market Scale
data.description:
Goldman Sachs , the global investment bank and asset manager, fell approximately 2.6% to $963.55 Tuesday even as its asset-management arm pulled in $11.7 billion across a fresh group of private-equity funds. The fundraising shows institutions are still willing to hand Goldman serious capital, but the stock reaction suggests investors wanted more than another strong fundraising headline.

The haul includes $9.6 billion for West Street Capital Partners IX, $1.6 billion for an Asia-focused strategy and another $500 million for co-investment vehicles. That puts roughly 82% of the total in the flagship fund, which has already deployed more than one-third of its capital. Goldman expects the money to be invested over roughly four to four-and-a-half years, giving the firm a long runway to convert commitments into investments, fees and eventually realizations.

Goldman Sachs Alternatives managed $459 billion at the end of June and is aiming for $750 billion by 2030, so this $11.7 billion raise represents about 2.5% of the current platform. The valuation picture is worth watching too: the shares at $963.55 sit 16.33% above the GuruFocus GF Value estimate of $828.31. That premium tells the story clearlyGoldman is still executing on fundraising, but investors are already paying well above the GF Value benchmark, raising the bar for deployment returns, exits and recurring fee growth.

data.title: WSJ Tech Council Summit: NASA's Isaacman Wants Agency to Get Back Its Mojo
data.description:
By Elias Schisgall

Jared Isaacman wants the National Aeronautics and Space Administration to regain its mojo.

The NASA administrator said the agency has lost its focus and ability to quickly execute in recent years. "We are just trying to get our swagger back here, get back in a rhythm of what we did" in the 1960s, Isaacman said at The Wall Street Journal's Technology Council Summit, calling that period NASA's "glory days."

"This is simply going back to the playbook that achieved these near-impossible outcomes from decades past," Isaacman said.

There is urgency, he said, to breathe life into the agency as the U.S. races China to establish a presence on the moon and secure valuable lunar real estate.

"There is a second space race. It will come down to months, not years. The Chinese will absolutely put their astronauts on the surface of the Moon, do what the Soviets never could," Isaacman said. "And I think the implications of that will be felt around the world."

Isaacman has tried to realize this shift by eliminating "needless bureaucracy" and flattening the agency's organizational structure, as well as by spending more time in the field himself.

He is also trying to bring more of NASA's workforce back in-house, after what he described as an extended period of outsourcing to contractors that contributed to higher costs and slower launch cadences.

Personnel for mission control and rocket designing, construction and launching should be brought within the agency, Isaacman said. And though NASA should continue to act as one customer of many for components and services that have a high level of technical readiness, he said the agency should be more hands-on for more ambitious projects, such as spacecraft fueled by nuclear power.

"We are course-correcting back to center on the balance between, what is the near-impossible--it doesn't have an obvious business or use case--that NASA should be doing, and where can you leverage industry to supplement, just as we did in the early days," Isaacman said. "I think we're getting back to the right balance there."

Write to Elias Schisgall at elias.schisgall@wsj.com

data.title: 2 charts showing how oil is becoming the market's biggest wild card
data.description:
By Isabel Wang

Crude is increasingly 'the straw that stirs the drink' of the current global macro risk regime, a Nomura strategist warns

Oil is becoming a bigger problem for both stocks and long-term bonds.

Oil is increasingly calling the tune in global markets, as rising energy prices and worries about how much consumers are paying at the gas pump are making investors nervous and affecting their portfolios.

Since the U.S.-Iran war began in late February, higher oil prices have been bad news for both stocks and long-term Treasury bonds. When crude prices jump, stocks tend to fall. The same is true for long-duration government debt, as higher oil prices have been accompanied by falling bond prices and, in turn, higher yields.

That relationship has become much stronger over the past seven months, as shown in the charts below.

The Iran war appears to have marked a turning point in the relationship between oil and both stocks and Treasurys. Before the war, the relationship between U.S. benchmark West Texas Intermediate crude (CL00) (CL.1) (CLV26) and the S&P 500 SPX was basically neutral, with their rolling 63-day correlation at just 0.04 on Feb. 27. But by the end of March, it had fallen to minus 0.35, and by late April it had reached minus 0.48, according to Dow Jones Market Data. In other words, when oil prices rise, stocks have increasingly tended to fall.

A value closer to minus 1 means a perfect negative correlation between oil prices and stocks, while a number closer to 0 shows the relationship is very weak or even nonexistent.

The same pattern is showing up in long-term Treasurys BX:TMUBMUSD10Y BX:TMUBMUSD30Y. The rolling 63-day correlation between the U.S. oil benchmark and the iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF TLT fell to minus 0.28 by the end of April, from minus 0.15 on Feb. 27. It was at minus 0.55 on Tuesday morning, according to Dow Jones Market Data.

"Crude oil and energy is 'the straw that stirs the drink' of the current global macro risk regime," said Charlie McElligott, cross-asset macro strategist at Nomura Securities International.

Indeed, oil is increasingly behaving like a macro risk for equities, rather than simply another indicator of economic growth. Normally, higher oil prices can be bullish for stocks because they can signal stronger economic demand. That's partly why the correlation between WTI and the S&P 500 was mostly positive in 2025.

But now, the oil supply shock brought on by the Middle East conflict is propelling energy prices higher as transportation and production costs rise. At the same time, central banks are fighting to keep interest rates higher for longer. That matters to U.S. households because higher rates would directly increase the cost of borrowing money for mortgages, car loans and credit cards. They can also eat into American businesses' bottom lines, squeezing corporate margins and weighing on equity valuations.

"Treasury yields are now impacted less by safe-haven flows and more by inflation expectations, and the correlation between yields and oil prices is at its highest level for seven years," said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB.

In other words, the oil shock is having a direct impact on U.S. financial conditions, Brooks told MarketWatch on Tuesday.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury note BX:TMUBMUSD10Y was up 2 basis points, to trade at 5.040%, its highest intraday level since July 19, 2007. The 30-year rate was also up 2 basis points, at 5.369%, according to FactSet data.

"I've always found it somewhat odd that front-month oil correlates so highly to the 10-year Treasury [yield], but their increasingly synchronized moves reflects not only inflation is at risk but real rates are backing up substantially," said Nate Shetty, chief investment officer at SEI Investments Company.

Real interest rates are nominal interest rates minus the inflation rate. When they rise substantially, it means money is genuinely becoming more expensive to borrow for U.S. consumers and businesses in terms of actual purchasing power.

"We are believers that Treasurys have lost their flight-to-quality positions," Shetty told MarketWatch in a phone interview on Tuesday. "In other words, the negative correlation we've seen in 20 years past between Treasurys and stocks has now flipped to the positive."

"Another way of saying this is that Treasurys are going to trade like risk assets, and in fact, they are," he said.

Of course, equities won't escape rising oil prices unscathed. "When the consequences of a geopolitical crisis roils oil markets and bruises the bond market, it is only a matter of time before equities get hit," Brooks of XTB added.

Opinion: Stocks have so far survived rising Treasury yields. But that may be about to change.

But aside from this week's tech selloff following calls from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and other executives to slow artificial-intelligence development, U.S. stocks have been resilient. The Dow Jones Industrial Average DJIA was off just 0.4% so far this quarter, while the S&P 500 has risen 1.2% and the Nasdaq Composite COMP was down 0.9%, according to FactSet data.

-Isabel Wang

data.title: Brent crude tops $109 as latest drone attacks, Iran tensions threaten key Saudi oil shipping routes
data.description:
New Delhi, Sept. 15 -- Crude oil prices resumed their upward move in Tuesday's session, with Brent crude futures surging $3.7 per barrel to $109.39 as traders assessed the potential impact on global crude supplies after Saudi Arabia closed a critical pipeline that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz last week.

Drones launched from Iraq damaged the East-West Pipeline on Thursday, forcing the Saudi government to shut the key crude oil artery. The pipeline is expected to remain largely out of service for weeks as repairs are carried out, The Associated Press reported, citing two regional officials.

The pipeline provides Saudi Arabia with an alternative route to transport oil exports to the Red Sea, allowing it to bypass the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, where Iranian attacks have disrupted the movement of oil tankers.

Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz - through which around a fifth of the world's traded oil and gas transits in peacetime - in the opening days of the war.

Since then, Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, for crude oil exports.

After the war began, the East-West Pipeline carried a large majority of Saudi Arabia's oil exports, AP reported, citing Rystad Energy, a Norway-based research firm. The disruption to the pipeline could therefore further complicate Saudi Arabia's efforts to move crude to international markets.

When Houthi attacks in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait began in late July, most tankers from the port of Yanbu turned north in the Red Sea towards the Mediterranean, sending their cargo through the Suez Canal or an Egyptian pipeline.

The pipeline has been carrying an average of 2.6 million to 4 million barrels per day since late August - a volume that could be lost to the market if its flow stops completely, according to an analysis issued Monday by Rystad Energy.

Last week, Riyadh notified OPEC's secretariat that its output tumbled by 1.9 million barrels a day to 6.238 million barrels a day, according to a monthly report from the organisation obtained by Bloomberg.

That is even lower than the previous wartime nadir reached in April and marks the lowest production figure reported by Saudi Arabia since the beginning of the Gulf War.

The pipeline attack has also added to regional tensions. A diplomatic meeting between Iran and Gulf Arab states to discuss the situation in the Strait of Hormuz, originally scheduled for Monday in Oman, was abruptly postponed following the attack.

For more than a month, the Houthis have been striking Saudi oil infrastructure and shipping in the Red Sea, increasing pressure on global oil prices and strengthening Iran's leverage in its war with the United States.

The Houthis have reportedly seized the strategic Perim Island in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait after taking the port city of Mokha on Yemen's western coast, adding to concerns over the security of another key route for global oil shipments.

(With inputs from Bloomberg and AP)

data.title: Beta Bionics Slides on Public Offering to Fund Insulin Patch Pump Commercialization
data.description:
By Katherine Hamilton

Shares of Beta Bionics slipped after the medical devices company said it proposed a $125 million underwritten public offering.

The stock declined 5.1%, to $18.25, in after-hours trading Tuesday, after closing up 15%. Through the close, shares were still down 37% this year.

The company said it would use the proceeds of the offering for general corporate purposes, which could include costs associated with commercializing its tubeless insulin patch pump Mint.

Mint-related expenses could include expanding manufacturing sites, increasing research and development, investing in product enhancements and taking advantage of potential strategic opportunities, Beta Bionics said.

The company plans to grant the underwriters of the offering a 30-day option to buy up to an additional $18.75 million.
